description_en: The domed Śiva temple, constructed in the 20th century, is located on a rocky promontory on the right bank of the Tilā Nadī river in Khalāchaur, south of Michāgāũ. To reach the temple, a flight of stairs ascends to the top of the promontory.Built on a platform with three central steps, the temple has a rectangular layout and is constructed using stone and mud masonry. The single door faces the northeast, while the cemented facade is on the northeast side. Within the sanctum, there is an elevated platform housing a damaged temple pinnacle and a stoneśivaliṅgaon ayoni. Both theśivaliṅgaand theyoniappear to be recent artifacts.The roof of the temple features two stepped levels of stone slabs, with the final level taking a cruciform shape. Atop the roof sits a massive elongated dome, which is cemented. However, it is likely that the dome is made of roughly cut stones of varying sizes, as observed at the nearby Michāgāũ Mai Thān (JUM0302).This architectural style, influenced by the neo-classical monuments of Lucknow and later introduced to the Kathmandu valley during the era of Bhimsen Thapa (1775-1839), can be found in two locations in the Jumla district: the present temple in Khalāchaur and the Michāgāũ Mai Thān (JUM0302). Niels Gutschow examined similar dome temples in Far-West Nepal and noted that they were all built between the 1940s and 1980s (Gutschow 1992). While the exact construction date of this temple is unknown, it is reasonable to suggest that it was built during the latter half of the 20th century.
monument_assessment: Good (very few light surface damages, renovated or repaired)
references: REFERENCES Gutschow, Niels, 1992, “The need to build a temple. Observations on building traditions in change in Western Nepal”, in Aspects of Nepalese Traditions , Bernhard Kolver (ed.). Stuttgart: Franz Steiner Verlag, pp. 97-121.
